item.title: Whistle-Blower Says Trump Officials Are Defying Court Orders on Voting by Mail
item.description: A report detailed “grave concerns” that a new system being rushed into use by the U.S. Postal Service could imperil millions of mail ballots ahead of the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Chris Cameron
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: The office of Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut, published the whistle-blower report on voting by mail.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial: Jury to Begin Fourth Day of Deliberations
item.description: Jurors have spent about 17 hours discussing the case over three days. They have several options for a verdict, ranging from not guilty to first-degree murder.
item.dc:creator: Maia Spoto
item.media:credit: Pool photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger
item.media:description: Lindsay Clancy watches jury members on Monday morning.

item.title: What to Watch in the Massachusetts Primary Election
item.description: Senator Edward Markey, who began his congressional career in 1976, faces a challenge from Representative Seth Moulton.
item.dc:creator: By
item.media:credit: Mel Musto for The New York Times; Josh Reynolds/Associated Press
item.media:description: Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton are up against one another in the Democratic primary for senator in Massachusetts.

item.title: Markey Leads Moulton in Polls of Senate Primary in Massachusetts
item.description: Senator Ed Markey had double digit leads in every poll of the Democratic primary for Senate in August after Seth Moulton briefly narrowed the gap this spring.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Soler
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times; Kevin Lamarque/Reuters

item.title: How the Supreme Court Locks Away Its Own History
item.description: Supreme Court justices could keep the court’s internal working papers hidden for decades. Our investigative reporter Jodi Kantor explains why those records matter — and what sealing them away means for our understanding of key decisions by the nation’s highest court.
item.dc:creator: Jodi Kantor, Nour Idriss, Alexandra Ostasiewicz, June Kim, Stephanie Swart, David Seekamp and Edward Vega

item.title: How the Supreme Court Locks Away Its Own History
item.description: After Justice Scalia died, the justices held private negotiations about locking away their papers. We may not see the ultimate record of the Roberts court for decades.
item.dc:creator: Jodi Kantor
item.media:credit: Illustration by Ben Denzer; images by Michael Lee/Getty and Paul Denzer

item.title: Vance Defends Approach to Antisemitism in Remarks to Jewish Conservatives
item.description: In private remarks, Vice President JD Vance explained why he engages with some influencers accused of antisemitism. He also urged the audience to help articulate why a strong relationship with Israel is in America’s interest.
item.dc:creator: Yair Rosenberg and Theodore Schleifer
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: Vice President JD Vance at The White House in July.

item.title: California Lawmakers Pass Ban on Shock Gloves
item.description: The California Legislature moved quickly to approve the legislation in an attempt to stop ICE agents from using the gloves. Local law enforcement agencies have come out against the bill.
item.dc:creator: Tim Arango
item.media:credit: Nikos Frazier/Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images
item.media:description: California Democrats moved quickly to try to ban shock gloves to prevent ICE officers from using them.

item.title: How the Pentagon Is Getting Into the Venezuelan Oil Business Under Trump
item.description: The Defense Department’s Office of Strategic Capital, founded by the Biden administration to give loans to bolster the U.S. defense industry, is helping lead President Trump’s oil deal.
item.dc:creator: Edward Wong, Rebecca F. Elliott and Anatoly Kurmanaev
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Adriana Loureiro Fernandez for The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump said his defense secretary and secretary of state reached an agreement with the Venezuelan government on securing billions of barrels of oil reserves “through a partnership with private business.”

item.title: Wendell Berry, Writer Who Extolled America’s Agrarian Past, Dies at 92
item.description: A Kentucky farmer, he railed against agribusiness and championed small family farms and the environment, winning widespread acclaim.
item.dc:creator: Robert D. McFadden
item.category: Look & See: A Portrait of Wendell Berry (Movie)
item.media:credit: Steve Hebert for The New York Times
item.media:description: Author Wendell Berry in 2012. The historian Page Smith hailed him as “a prophetic American voice of our day.”

item.title: Trump Mocks Data-Center Opponents as Wanting to Stay ‘Backwards and Poor’
item.description: The giant computing sites that power A.I. are increasingly opposed by communities across the country, a signal of voters’ concern about a changing economy.
item.dc:creator: Luke Broadwater
item.media:credit: Ivan Pierre Aguirre for The New York Times
item.media:description: A 1,000-acre data center for Meta under construction in El Paso, Texas, in May. Polling shows most Americans oppose the proliferation of data centers in their communities.

item.title: Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll Resigns as U.S. Military Grapples With Two Wars
item.description: The resignation of Daniel P. Driscoll, the secretary of the Army, had been expected but comes at a tumultuous time for the service.
item.dc:creator: Helene Cooper and Greg Jaffe
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Haiyun Jiang for The New York Times
item.media:description: Daniel P. Driscoll, the secretary of the Army, had clashed with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

item.title: Defendants in Minnesota Church Protest Case Challenge Charges in Flurry of Motions
item.description: In their broadest assault yet against the charges, lawyers for the defendants pointed to the unusual investigative tactics the administration deployed to make the case against them.
item.dc:creator: Alan Feuer
item.media:credit: Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times
item.media:description: Demonstrators disrupted a church service at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minn., in January to protest the dual roles of one of its pastors, who also serves as an acting field director for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

item.title: JD Vance Called Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed ‘Evil’ in Speech
item.description: Vice President JD Vance also told Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, to “keep my wife’s name out of your mouth.”
item.dc:creator: Bayliss Wagner
item.media:credit: Paul Sancya/Associated Press
item.media:description: Vice President JD Vance’s remarks at a campaign rally on Monday appeared aimed at stoking tensions in Michigan’s Jewish community over Dr. El-Sayed’s nomination.

item.title: Scott Brown Was a GOP Star. Will It Matter in the New Hampshire Senate Race?
item.description: Scott Brown is chasing the political limelight again with a seemingly improvised Senate campaign.

item.media:credit: Aleksandra Michalska/Reuters

item.title: U.S. Strikes May Have Targeted a New Type of Iranian Naval Mine
item.description: The U.S. military said its attacks against Iran were in response to a threat to the Strait of Hormuz.
item.dc:creator: John Ismay
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Reuters
item.media:description: Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz seen from Musandam, Oman, on Monday. The strait has been under constant threat since the United States and Israel launched a combined assault against Iran on Feb. 28.

item.title: Teen Charged With Murder After Livestreaming San Diego Mosque Shooting
item.description: The authorities said the 17-year-old from North Carolina had recorded the attack, which killed three people in May. “She ran with the pack — she shared in the kill,” the district attorney said.
item.dc:creator: Eduardo Medina and Madaleine Rubin
item.media:credit: John Francis Peters for The New York Times
item.media:description: A memorial in front of the Islamic Center of San Diego, the day after a deadly shooting in May.

item.title: Bessent Claims Canada Is Too Small to Fight a Trade War With the U.S.
item.description: At gathering of G20 finance ministers, the Treasury secretary accused Canada’s prime minister of starting a “political shouting match” over U.S. trade policies.
item.dc:creator: Alan Rappeport
item.media:credit: Carlos Osorio/Reuters
item.media:description: The newly opened Gordie Howe International Bridge, linking Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, last month. Both the United States and Canada have announced high tariffs on each other’s products.

item.title: Supreme Court Allows Trump’s White House Ballroom Construction
item.description: Lower-court rulings would have blocked construction of the 90,000-square-foot ballroom after finding that the Trump administration should have first sought approval from Congress.
item.dc:creator: Ann E. Marimow
item.category: White House East Wing and Ballroom (Washington, DC)
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: The order from the Supreme Court was the second time in less than two weeks that the court weighed in on the project.

item.title: Kalshi Suspends Republican House Candidate for Betting on Her Own Race
item.description: The trading platform Kalshi issued a three-year suspension to the candidate, Laurie Buckhout, and fined her nearly $2,600. Ms. Buckhout said she had made a “dumb mistake.”
item.dc:creator: Kellen Browning
item.media:credit: Chris Seward/Associated Press
item.media:description: Laurie Buckhout, a former U.S. Army colonel and a Republican, is challenging Representative Don Davis of North Carolina.
